title: What are common replication topologies: single-primary + read replicas, multi-primary/active-active (conflict resolution needed), cascading replication (replica feeds another replica): and when do you use each?
shortTitle: Common replication topologies and when to use each
keyPoints: Single-primary with read replicas sends all writes to one node and fans reads to replicas for horizontal read scaling.
Single-primary keeps writes simple and consistent, with replicas serving as failover candidates.
Multi-primary (active-active) accepts writes on more than one node, requiring conflict detection and resolution.
Conflict resolution strategies include last-write-wins, per-column merge, and application-level reconciliation.
Cascading replication has a replica forward changes to downstream replicas, reducing WAL fan-out load on the primary.
Banks avoid active-active for the core ledger because money cannot tolerate conflicting writes.
Most systems start single-primary and only adopt multi-primary when multi-region write availability is a hard requirement.

s1_definition.oneliner: Single-primary for most apps (simple, read scaling); multi-primary only when you truly need multi-region writes (and accept conflict resolution); cascading to offload fan-out from the primary.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Single-primary + read replicas** – all writes go to one primary; reads fan out to replicas for scaling; replicas can be promoted on failover.
- **Multi-primary (active-active)** – multiple nodes accept writes; requires conflict detection and resolution (last-write-wins, CRDTs, application logic).
- **Cascading replication** – a replica forwards changes to downstream replicas, forming a tree that reduces load on the primary.
- **Conflict resolution** – the mechanism to reconcile divergent writes when two nodes modify the same row; the hard part of multi-primary.
- **Read-your-writes** – a consistency concern with single-primary: a client that writes to the primary and immediately reads from a replica may see stale data.
s1_definition.analogy: Single-primary is one National Bank of India head office that records every change and mails copies to branches for reading. Multi-primary is several branches all allowed to write at once: powerful but risky, because two branches might change Rajesh's record differently and you must reconcile. Cascading is a regional hub that receives from head office and relays to its own sub-branches, so head office is not overwhelmed.

sections.s2_detail:
### What is single-primary with read replicas?

One writable primary handles all writes. Several read-only replicas serve read traffic and can be promoted on failover. This is the default topology for most applications.

```sql
-- Application connection routing
-- Writes: always go to the primary
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 25000.00
WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001';  -- primary

-- Reads: routed to a replica (round-robin)
SELECT balance FROM accounts
WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001';  -- replica
```

```java
package com.bank.config;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.util.logging.Logger;

public class ReadWriteRoutingConfig {

    private static final Logger LOG = Logger.getLogger(
        ReadWriteRoutingConfig.class.getName());

    private final DataSource primaryDataSource;
    private final DataSource replicaDataSource;

    public ReadWriteRoutingConfig(DataSource primary, DataSource replica) {
        this.primaryDataSource = primary;
        this.replicaDataSource = replica;
    }

    public DataSource getWriteDataSource() {
        LOG.fine("Routing write to primary");
        return primaryDataSource;
    }

    public DataSource getReadDataSource() {
        LOG.fine("Routing read to replica");
        return replicaDataSource;
    }

    public DataSource getReadAfterWriteDataSource() {
        // For read-your-writes consistency, route to primary
        LOG.fine("Read-after-write: routing to primary");
        return primaryDataSource;
    }
}
```

### What are the limits of single-primary?

The limits are replica lag (read-your-writes needs care) and a single write bottleneck. All writes must go through one node, so write throughput is capped by that node's capacity.

```text
Single-Primary Limits:

  Writes: all go to one node (bottleneck at high write volume)
  Reads: scale horizontally across replicas
  Lag: replica may be behind by milliseconds to seconds
  Read-your-writes: Rajesh deposits money, then immediately
    reads balance from a replica that has not received the
    write yet. Solution: route read-after-write to primary.
```

### What is multi-primary (active-active) replication?

Multi-primary lets multiple nodes accept writes. This is useful for low-latency writes across regions or continuous availability. The hard part is conflict resolution.

```text
Multi-Primary Conflict Scenario:

  Node A (Delhi)              Node B (Mumbai)
  ┌──────────────┐            ┌──────────────┐
  │ UPDATE       │            │ UPDATE       │
  │ Rajesh name  │            │ Rajesh name  │
  │ = 'Raj K.'   │            │ = 'R. Kumar' │
  └──────┬───────┘            └──────┬───────┘
         │       Replicate            │
         └────────────────────────────┘
         CONFLICT: which name wins?
```

```sql
-- Conflict resolution strategies:

-- 1. Last-write-wins (timestamp-based)
-- The write with the latest timestamp wins
-- Simple but can lose data silently

-- 2. Per-column merge
-- If Node A changed name and Node B changed email,
-- merge both changes (no conflict)

-- 3. Application-level reconciliation
-- Queue conflicting writes for manual or automated resolution
```

### Why do banks avoid active-active for the core ledger?

Money cannot tolerate conflicting writes. If two nodes both debit Rajesh's account simultaneously, the balance can go wrong. Banks prefer single-primary for the ledger and partition writes by region if multi-region is needed.

```java
package com.bank.service;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.logging.Logger;

/**
 * Why active-active is dangerous for money:
 * Two concurrent withdrawals at different nodes
 * can both succeed, violating the balance invariant.
 */
public class ActiveActiveRisk {

    private static final Logger LOG = Logger.getLogger(
        ActiveActiveRisk.class.getName());

    public void demonstrateRisk() {
        // Node A (Delhi): Rajesh withdraws 80000
        // Node B (Mumbai): Rajesh withdraws 80000
        // Balance: 100000
        //
        // Both nodes check: 100000 >= 80000? Yes.
        // Both nodes debit: 100000 - 80000 = 20000.
        // Replication merges: balance = 20000 on both nodes.
        // But actual withdrawals: 80000 + 80000 = 160000.
        // Real balance should be: 100000 - 160000 = -60000.
        // Money was created out of thin air.

        LOG.severe("Active-active for money is unsafe without "
            + "global coordination (which defeats the purpose)");
    }
}
```

### What is cascading replication?

Cascading replication has a replica act as an upstream for further replicas, forming a tree. This reduces WAL fan-out pressure on the primary when there are many replicas or cross-region hops.

```text
Cascading Topology:

  Primary (Delhi)
     │
     ├──► Replica 1 (Delhi local)
     │
     └──► Replica 2 (Mumbai hub)
              │
              ├──► Replica 3 (Mumbai local)
              │
              └──► Replica 4 (Chennai local)

  Primary sends WAL to 2 replicas instead of 4.
  Mumbai hub relays to its own downstream replicas.
```

```sql
-- PostgreSQL: cascading replication setup
-- Replica 2 connects to Primary
-- primary_conninfo = 'host=primary port=5432'

-- Replica 3 connects to Replica 2 (not Primary)
-- primary_conninfo = 'host=replica2 port=5432'

-- Replica 2 must have hot_standby = on
-- to allow downstream replicas to connect
```

### How do the topologies compare?

| Aspect | Single-Primary | Multi-Primary | Cascading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Write nodes | 1 | Multiple | 1 |
| Conflict risk | None | High | None |
| Read scaling | Good (add replicas) | Good | Good |
| Write scaling | Limited (one node) | Good (multiple) | Limited |
| Complexity | Low | High | Medium |
| Use case | Most apps | Multi-region writes | Many replicas / regions |

### When should you use each topology?

Start single-primary and add read replicas. Use cascading when the replica count or geography strains the primary. Adopt multi-primary only when multi-region write availability is a hard requirement and the data model tolerates conflicts.

```text
Decision Guide:

  Question                              Topology
  ────────────────────────────────────  ────────────────────
  Standard app, read scaling needed?    Single-primary
  Many replicas, cross-region reads?    Cascading
  Must write in multiple regions?       Multi-primary
  Data is money or has hard invariant?  Single-primary always
```

### What should a senior engineer know?

A senior should know that even "multi-primary" setups in banking often partition writes by region (Delhi accounts write to Delhi, Mumbai accounts write to Mumbai) to avoid conflicts entirely, achieving geographic write locality without true conflict resolution.

```text
Partitioned-Write Pattern (bank-safe "multi-region"):

  Delhi Primary          Mumbai Primary
  ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────┐
  │ Accounts     │       │ Accounts     │
  │ DEL-*        │       │ MUM-*        │
  └──────────────┘       └──────────────┘
  Writes for Delhi       Writes for Mumbai
  accounts only          accounts only

  No conflict: each account has exactly one writer.
  Cross-region reads via replication for any account.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The three common replication topologies are single-primary with read replicas, multi-primary or active-active, and cascading replication. Single-primary sends all writes to one writable node and fans reads to read-only replicas, which keeps writes simple and consistent while scaling reads and giving failover candidates. Its limits are replica lag and the single write bottleneck.

Multi-primary accepts writes on more than one node for multi-region write availability, but it demands conflict detection and resolution because two nodes can change the same row differently. Cascading replication lets a replica forward changes to downstream replicas, offloading fan-out from the primary at the cost of extra lag per hop.

At the National Bank of India, the core ledger is deliberately single-primary because money cannot tolerate conflicting writes. All balance updates go to one writable node and reporting reads are routed round-robin across replicas. For the far region, Pankaj uses a cascading replica that streams from a nearby replica rather than the primary. The team only considers active-active when multi-region low-latency writes are a hard requirement, and even then they partition writes by region to avoid conflicts entirely.

The decision guide is: start single-primary for most workloads, use cascading to relieve fan-out when replica count or geography grows, and adopt active-active only when multi-region writes are mandatory and conflict resolution is acceptable.

Remember one sentence: single-primary for most workloads, cascading to relieve fan-out, and active-active only when multi-region writes are mandatory and conflict resolution is acceptable.
